Join us for a special three-part book club exploring the poetry of Joy Harjo in conversation with the art of Athena LaTocha, co-hosted by Jones Library and the University Museum of Contemporary Art.

event.title: Introduction to Restorative & Transformative Justice: Seeding Restorative Mindset in the UMass Amherst Community
event.stream_info: Registrants will recieve a Zoom link and outlook calendar invitation, after Registering at this link.
event.description:
In a dominant culture increasingly defined by dynamics of ideological polarization, emotionally-armored conflict, inter- and intra-community call-outs and cancellation campaigns, Restorative and Transformative Justice can offer alternate paths toward principled struggle, intentional repair, collective healing, and coalition building. 

 

In this interactive workshop, participants will be invited to root into their own unique core values while learning about the historical origins of restorative practices, as well as some key vocabulary, core concepts, and essential inquiries that inform and support such practices. In addition to articulating our vision(s) for a restorative future, we will also consider the ways in which punitive/carceral mindset currently functions within ourselves and our communities, identifying action items to invite greater alignment with our hopes and goals for growth and evolution. 

 

While this session is intended to be accessible to those who are brand new to RJ/TJ, seasoned practitioners and those with existing deep knowledge are welcome and invited to add their energy and voices to this whole-community conversation!

 

Presented by:

Rita Curley (she/her), Senior Investigator in the Equal Opportunity & Access Office

Penn Pritchard (they/them), Senior Director for Education & Development in the Office of Equity & Inclusion

Cas Rego-Martin (they/he), Education Coordinator in the Office of Equity & Inclusion

event.title: Distinguished Faculty Lecture Series: Jianhan Chen
event.description:
The Orderly Chaos of Proteins

 

For decades, we believed that every protein in our bodies requires a stable, well-defined 3D structure to function, but we have recently discovered a hidden world of biological “shape-shifters” that defy conventional wisdom. These Intrinsically Disordered Proteins (IDPs) are the “dark matter” of our cells, existing not as stable shapes but as shifting and apparently chaotic clouds of dynamic conformations. IDPs masterfully control our most complex cellular decisions and even form mysterious “liquid droplets” that organize major cellular processes. While this flexibility is essential for life, it also has a dangerous side. When these shape-shifters go awry, they become the primary drivers of devastating diseases like Alzheimer’s and cancers, where they represent a staggering two-thirds of all cancer-associated proteins. In this lecture, Professor Jianhan Chen will explore the fascinating ways that nature has been able to take advantage of the apparent “chaos” of IDPs for function and how we are using computational modeling as “digital microscopes” to decode this functional chaos, showing that understanding these fascinating molecules is the key to unlocking the next generation of life-saving medicines.

event.title: Talking Tech: Reduce Your Cyber-risk
event.description:
Sponsored by Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences and the Public Interest Technology Initiative at UMass, Talking Tech aims to demystify the technology that drives our world.

 

Wednesday, October 7, 5:30pm: Predicting Elections: Why Can’t We Get It Right? 

Our technologies for analyzing data and building models of user behavior have evolved dramatically. Yet election polls are frequently poor predictors of election results. Why? Just in time for the November election, Fran and Laura talk about the many sources of uncertainty in the prediction process, and why even the best forecasters and pundits can be wrong. 

 

Wednesday, November 4, 5:30pm: Has Your Behavior Been Hacked? 

Companies spend mega-bucks on so-called “behavioral engineering” and “psychographic targeting” (used by Cambridge Analytica in the 2016 election). You’re aware of standard ads and marketing, but technology has enabled whole new ways for companies, influencers, and social media to sway you. Be informed for the holidays! 

 

Wednesday, December 2, 5:30pm: Reduce Your Cyber-Risk 

We hear every day about a new danger or risk in cyberspace. Phishing, scams, hacks leading to identity theft, ransomware and malware, oh, my! Not to mention stories about surveillance and stalking, child exploitation, chatbots giving harmful advice, and general misinformation. What can you do to lower your risk and get the benefits of our amazing modern technology with less fear? Fran and Laura will provide practical advice in this interactive session. Come with questions!

 

About the Hosts 

 

Francine Berman is Director of Public Interest Technology in the Manning College of Computer and Information Sciences at UMass, as well as a Faculty Associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University. Berman is a leader in the field of Public Interest Technology, focused on the responsible development, use and management of technology for social impact. Berman received the 2024 Pioneer in Tech award from the National Center for Women in Technology and is a regular panelist on WAMC’s Roundtable. 

 

Laura Haas is Professor and former Dean of the Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences at UMass. Haas was formerly an IBM Fellow, leading research and development in data management and data science. She is a member of the National Academy of Engineering, a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and currently chairs the National Academies’ Computer Science and Telecommunications Board.

event.title: Feminist Movements Confronting Oligarchy
event.description:
Feinberg Series Panel with Elisabeth Armstrong and Emily Callaci

 

Who has value and who doesn’t? In the face of an economic system that considers most of the world’s population disposable, how have some social movements challenged capitalist definitions of value? This panel explores the feminist and anticapitalist Wages for Housework movement of the 1970s. Questions about gender, labor, interdependence, social reproduction, and care work—especially when considered in a global context—challenge key premises of capitalist oligarchy. What can we learn from the history of these social movements? How can they help us confront oligarchy in the present to build a future where all people have value, not only the few?

 

Panelists

Elisabeth Armstrong is the Sydenham Clark Parsons Professor of Women, Gender & Sexuality Studies at Smith College. She is the author of two books about the Left women's movement in India and across Asia; Gender and Neoliberalism: The All India Democratic Women's Association and its Strategies of Resistance and Bury the Corpse of Colonialism: The Revolutionary Feminist Conference of 1949. Her current project is on anticolonialism and propaganda in the internationalist youth and students movement, the World Federation of Democratic Youth.

 

Emily Callaci is a feminist historian, writer, and professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Her recent book is called Wages for Housework: The Feminist Fight Against Unpaid Labor.

 

Elizabeth Jacob (moderator) is an assistant professor of African history at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. event.title: Maria Mazzotta
event.description:
Italian singer-songwriter Maria Mazzotta spent much of her career celebrating and exploring the nuances of the traditional music of her home region, Apulia’s Salento peninsula, first as a member of the internationally renowned ensemble Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino, then in her early solo work.

 

Mazzotta’s 2020 album, Amoreamaro, is both a gorgeous collection of open, emotional performances and a fascinating document of a musician and composer exploring the edges of a tradition awash in international influence. Mazzotta’s music on that effort ventures out from Salento (the heel of Italy’s boot) finding influences from across the Adriatic, Ionian, and Mediterranean, and shaping a sound at once fundamentally Pugliese and intriguingly international.

 

On her most recent release, 2024’s Onde, Mazzotta tears up whatever was left of her initial script to deliver a profoundly brilliant work in which Salentino tradition forms the foundation of a sound that not only pulls influence from southern Europe and northern Africa but layers in fuzzy, gritty post-rock experimentation. Mazzotta, along with percussionist Cristiano Della Monica and guitarist Ernesto Nobili, set out to create a collection of songs that move and vary like the sea (onde translates to waves). And they accomplished exactly that, capturing the calm, the fury, the raw power, and the infinite changeability of tides in a collection of traditional and original songs that is impossible to set aside. Entrancing, captivating, enveloping, Onde pulls the listener in and works its will in a manner that reflects Mazzotta’s live performances. With her commanding voice and dynamic stage presence, Mazzotta makes every concert an immersive experience. Join us to see, hear, and feel it for yourself.

event.title: New England Civic Architecture & Public Literacy Sanctuaries: Boston Public Library Historic Study
event.description:
This public humanities and architectural history seminar explores the foundational role of monumental civic libraries as democratic palaces of public literacy, quiet contemplative study, and open municipal memory throughout New England. Focusing on the historic McKim Building of the Boston Public Library at Copley Square, the session analyzes how late nineteenth-century Beaux-Arts civic architecture embodied the motto 'Free to All,' creating grand communal reading spaces like Bates Hall that democratized access to world scholarship. Architectural historians, library science scholars, and cultural preservationists examine the integration of public murals, courtyard sanctuaries, and carved granite inscriptions that set the architectural benchmark for civic educational institutions across America.

Incorporating archival documentation, visitor circulation studies, and spatial preservation insights from the Things To Do Radar Boston Public Library Visiting Guide, the presentation investigates how public institutions balance historic architectural preservation with modern digital accessibility and community assembly needs. The seminar concludes with an interactive panel on the future of municipal reading palaces as essential civic third places. All university students, faculty, and Pioneer Valley community members are warmly invited to attend.

event.description:
UMass Professor of Piano Gilles Vonsattel is in the midst of a multi-year journey through one of the most challenging and important catalogs in the classical music canon, traveling from coast to coast, performing all 32 of Beethoven’s piano sonatas in a series of concerts at prestigious venues in New York and California. 

 

He is also bringing that tour to campus in a series of eight free concerts  showcasing these brilliant compositions and his mastery of his craft.

 

All concerts are in Bezanson Recital Hall and start at 7:30 PM. All free to attend!

 

October 22nd: Sonata No. 1 in F minor for Piano, Op. 2, No. 1  (1795), Sonata No. 21 in C major for Piano, Op. 53, "Waldstein" (1803-04), Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major for Piano, Op. 106, "Hammerklavier" (1817-18)

 

October 29th: Sonata #4, Op. 7 "Grand Sonata", Sonata #8, Op. 13 "Pathetique" and Sonata #11 Op. 22.

 

November 19th: Sonata #25, Op. 79 "Cuckoo", Sonata #3, Op. 2, No. 3, Sonata #19, Op. 49, No. 1, Sonata #22, Op. 54, Sonata #31, No. 2 "The Tempest"


December 16th: #10 Op. 14 No. 2, #7 Op. 10 No. 3, #13 Op. 27 Quasi una fantasia, #14 Op. 27 No. 2 Moonlight

  • February 26
  • March 6

event.title: Winter Solstice at the UMass Sunwheel
event.description:
The public is invited to observe sunrise and sunset on the day of the winter solstice among the standing stones of the UMass Amherst Sunwheel on Sunday, Dec. 21, at 7 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. Faculty from the UMass Amherst astronomy department will discuss the astronomical cause of the solstice, and a telescope will be set up to observe the waning gibbous moon, Venus, and the surface of the sun. Heavy rain or snow will cancel the gatherings.

 

  • Sunrise gathering 7:00 a.m.
  • Sunset gathering 3:30 p.m.

 

The UMass Amherst Sunwheel is located south of McGuirk Alumni Stadium, just off Rocky Hill Road (Amity Street) about one-quarter mile south of University Drive. Visitors to the Sunwheel should be prepared for freezing temperatures and wet footing. Rain or blizzard conditions cancel the events. Donations are welcome to help with the cost of additional site work and future events.

event.title: Faculty Concert Series: Gilles Vonsattel Plays Beethoven's Piano Sonatas
event.description:
UMass Professor of Piano Gilles Vonsattel is in the midst of a multi-year journey through one of the most challenging and important catalogs in the classical music canon, traveling from coast to coast, performing all 32 of Beethoven’s piano sonatas in a series of concerts at prestigious venues in New York and California. 

 

He is also bringing that tour to campus in a series of eight free concerts  showcasing these brilliant compositions and his mastery of his craft.

 

All concerts are in Bezanson Recital Hall and start at 7:30 PM. All free to attend!

 

October 22nd: Sonata No. 1 in F minor for Piano, Op. 2, No. 1  (1795), Sonata No. 21 in C major for Piano, Op. 53, "Waldstein" (1803-04), Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major for Piano, Op. 106, "Hammerklavier" (1817-18)

 

October 29th: Sonata #4, Op. 7 "Grand Sonata", Sonata #8, Op. 13 "Pathetique" and Sonata #11 Op. 22.

 

November 19th: Sonata #25, Op. 79 "Cuckoo", Sonata #3, Op. 2, No. 3, Sonata #19, Op. 49, No. 1, Sonata #22, Op. 54, Sonata #31, No. 2 "The Tempest"


December 16th: #10 Op. 14 No. 2, #7 Op. 10 No. 3, #13 Op. 27 Quasi una fantasia, #14 Op. 27 No. 2 Moonlight

 

Spring Concerts (Repertoire to be Announced)

  • January 22
  • February 26
  • March 6
  • March 22
